newsitem.title: USA: U.S. YIELD CURVE -- 10-year seen underperforming.
newsitem.headline: U.S. YIELD CURVE -- 10-year seen underperforming.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury yield curve's new theme could be "whatever comes down must go up," if you believe analysts who foresee the steepening of a number of spreads which have tightened dramatically in recent months.
For instance, the tight spread of eight basis points between the five-year note (at 6.07 percent) and 10-year note (6.15 percent), has raised a few eyebrows.
Only six weeks ago the spread was twice as wide, and it had hovered between 20 and 25 basis points in February and early March.
In the very near future, analysts predicted, the 10-year should begin to reverse its recent trend and underperform the rest of the market.
"The 10-year is rich," said Larry Dyer, Treasury market strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston Corp. "If history is a guide, owning anything but 10-years will make you money.
"I am recommending (clients) buying fives and 30s against the 10-year," he added.
Dyer and other analysts forecast a 10-basis point steepening of the five-year to 10-year spread to a more normal level of around 18 basis points.
At the same time, analysts noted that the spread between the 10-year note and 30-year bond has room to narrow from its current 27 basis points to as little as 15 basis points.
Bond yields are seen falling to around 6.25 percent from the current 6.43 percent, while 10-year notes look likely to decline to only about 6.10 percent, analysts said.
"It seems like everyone wants to own the long bond," said Richard Suttmeier, chief financial strategist at William R. Hough & Co.

Over the past month or so, analysts said, the 10-year note was propped up by flows from mortgage-backed securities. The so-called convexity flow, due to the lower MBS rates and fears of increased mortgage refinancings, should stop or slow down to the point where it has no discernible impact, they predicted.

Also enhancing the 10-year's premium was the Treasury's announcement last month that it was cutting two regular 10-year note auctions this year. The anticipation lower supply drove 10-year note prices higher, analysts said.

The current economic landscape -- the Federal Reserve apparently on hold for now with a tightening down the road, low inflation and a rapidly falling federal budget deficit -- should encourage investors to buy 30-year bonds, analysts forecast.
With two-year note yields just 35 basis points over the 5.5-percent federal funds rate, investors are starting to look further out the curve for value, analysts said.
"It is hard to imagine how the short end can move much farther until it prices out a (future) Fed tightening move," said Steven Slifer, chief economist at Lehman Brothers.
"But bond yields can go to 6.25 percent," he added, "if we continue to to see the (annual federal) budget deficit $40 billion and lower."
